What is a Civil Case under Nepalese Law? Definition, Legal Scope & Remedies

📅 Published: 2025-01-15
🔄 Updated: 2025-10-01
⏱ 7 min read
🔍 Review: Senior Advocate Lead Counsel, Supreme Court Bar Association
Direct Legal Answer & Overview

Under Nepalese jurisprudence and the National Civil Code 2074 (मुलुकी देवानी संहिता, २०७४), a civil case (Dewani Mudda) is a judicial proceeding initiated by an individual or legal entity before a court to establish, enforce, or recover a private civil right, obtain compensation for harm (Kshatipurti), or restrain an unlawful interference through an injunction. Unlike criminal prosecution, civil suits aim to restore the aggrieved party to their rightful position rather than inflict penal punishment.

Key Practical Takeaways

  • Civil disputes focus on private legal rights, contracts, property titles, inheritance, and personal relations.
  • The plaintiff (Firdi) initiates the case by filing a Plaint (Firdi-patra) and bears the primary burden of proof.
  • Primary legal remedies include monetary recovery, specific performance, cancellation of fraudulent deeds, and injunctions.
  • Governed by the Muluki Civil Code 2074 and Muluki Civil Procedure Code 2074.

In Nepalese law, the distinction between civil and criminal matters is fundamental to selecting the correct court, procedural timetable, and legal strategy. A civil case—known in Nepali as Dewani Mudda (देवानी मुद्दा)—is concerned with the enforcement, determination, and protection of private individual and commercial rights.

1. The Statutory Definition of a Civil Dispute in Nepal

Following the major legal reforms of 2074 BS (2017/2018 CE), Nepalese civil jurisprudence was codified under two monumental statutes: the Muluki Civil Code 2074 (substantive civil rights) and the Muluki Civil Procedure Code 2074 (procedural court rules).

Under Section 15 of the Civil Code, any person whose civil right is infringed, denied, or threatened by another party is entitled to seek judicial remedies before the competent court of law. Unlike criminal offenses where the state acts to punish public wrongs against society, a civil action is entirely private in character.

2. Key Distinctions: Civil Lawsuit vs. Criminal Case

Attribute Civil Case (Dewani Mudda) Criminal Case (Faujdari Mudda)
Initiating Party Private individual, enterprise, or entity (Plaintiff / Firdi) State Prosecutor / Police or Private Complainant
Primary Objective Enforce rights, recover debt, cancel void deeds, or get damages Punish the offender via imprisonment, fines, or community service
Standard of Proof Preponderance of evidence / Balance of probabilities Proof beyond reasonable doubt
Burden of Proof Lies upon the party asserting the civil right (Section 25, Evidence Act) Lies upon the State prosecution (Section 26, Evidence Act)
Court Forum District Court Civil Bench, High Court, Supreme Court District Court Criminal Bench, Special Court, High Court

3. Common Categories of Civil Cases in Nepal Courts

Civil disputes in Nepal typically fall into five broad legal categories:

  • Contractual Disputes: Claims arising from the non-performance of written contracts, supply agreements, leases, or loans under promissory notes (Tamassuk).
  • Immovable Property Suits: Partition of ancestral holdings (Anshabanda), boundary demarcation disputes, title cancellation (Likhit Badr), and adverse possession challenges.
  • Family & Matrimonial Matters: Contested divorce (Sambandh Bichhed), child custody, spousal maintenance (Kharacha), and guardianship declarations.
  • Tort & Compensation Claims: Civil actions seeking damages (Kshatipurti) for negligence, property trespass, defamation, or nuisance under Part 6 of the Civil Code.
  • Injunction Suits: Petitions seeking urgent court orders (Nishedhajna) to restrain an opposing party from demolishing structures, selling disputed land, or violating easements.

4. Procedural Safeguards & Settlement Options

A distinctive feature of modern Nepalese civil procedure is the statutory preference for reconciliation. Under Section 193 of the Muluki Civil Procedure Code 2074, District Courts have a legal mandate to explore court-annexed mediation before commencing trial. If parties execute a settlement deed (Milapatra), the dispute concludes immediately with the full legal effect of a final court decree.

Statutory Citations & Governing Nepal Legislation

Statute / Act Section / Rule Legal Significance
Muluki Civil Code 2074 Section 15 (Protection of Civil Rights) Affirms every citizen right to institute civil proceedings for protection of legal rights.
Muluki Civil Procedure Code 2074 Chapter 3 (Institution of Lawsuits) Prescribes formal plaint filing requirements, court fees, and jurisdiction.

Documentary Checklist for this Procedure

  • ✔ Official Plaint (Firdi-patra) drafted in statutory court format
  • ✔ Proof of legal cause of action (contracts, receipts, promissory notes)
  • ✔ Copy of plaintiff Citizenship Certificate or corporate registration certificate
  • ✔ Receipt of statutory court fee (Court Fee Act 2017) deposit

Frequently Asked Questions on this Topic

Can a civil lawsuit in Nepal be converted into a criminal case?

Generally no, but if an underlying transaction involves intentional fraud (Thagi), document forgery (Kirtiye), or criminal breach of trust, the aggrieved party may lodge a separate First Information Report (FIR) under the Muluki Criminal Code alongside their civil recovery plaint.

What is the statutory limitation period (Hadmyad) to file a civil suit?

Limitation periods in Nepal vary by cause of action under the Muluki Civil Procedure Code 2074—commonly ranging from 6 months for injunctions and contract cancellations to 2 years for general money claims, and specific periods for partition.
